extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in race, media, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing practices, representations, controversies, and institutional responses related to blackface and its modern digital and cultural variants across media, performance, and public life. Covers definitions, historical context, authenticity debates, and international instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wigging (stunt doubles standing in across gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of a male performer portraying standing-in for a female actor is known as "wigging"; white men are the main source of stunt doubles in American TV and film productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a production practice where gender is crossed for stunt work; relevant when evaluating casting choices, representation, and whether stunt work erases or substitutes for actors of the same gender. Example/concern: critique of predominance of white male stunt doubles standing in for women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint down (stunt performers made up as another race)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the stunt performer is made up to look like another race, the practice is called a "paint down"; some stunt performers have equated it with blackface minstrelsy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flags a racialized make-up practice in production that may reproduce historic racist conventions. Use this term to evaluate whether production practices are racially insensitive or replicative of blackface; note industry actors' voices equating it to blackface have been cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital blackface / high-tech blackface
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital media provide opportunities to inhabit and perform Black identity without actually painting one's face; Adam Clayton Powell III coined the term "high-tech blackface" (1999) to refer to stereotypical portrayals of black characters in video games. Critics argue players perform a type of identity tourism by controlling Black avatars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to judge online representations and interactions: does a digital practice (avatar use, character design, game portrayal) reproduce or profit from stereotypical, commodified, or performative versions of Blackness? Examples: sports-game avatars, video-game portrayals. Theoretical framing includes identity tourism and constrained versions of blackness legible to white supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIFs, emojis, Bitmoji and 'online imagined Black English' as digital blackface
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-Black people sharing animated images or GIFs of Black people or Black-skinned emojis has been criticized as "digital blackface." Writers noted GIFs of women of color are frequently used to express emotions online; Bitmoji uses "black emotional reactions" designed to fit non-Black bodies. Manuel Arturo Abreu calls non-Black users' engagement in AAVE on the internet "online imagined Black English."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instances where users adopt Black-stereotyped expressive resources (GIFs, emojis, AAVE) without context or understanding. Anti-patterns: using GIFs of Black people as shorthand for emotion, adopting AAVE performatively, deploying Bitmoji/emoji designs that borrow Black-coded expression to fit non-Black users. Consider power/commodity dynamics and whether the practice echoes minstrelsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing, content advisory, and warnings when showing blackface in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argued showing films containing blackface without substantial framing, content advisory and a focus on its inherent racism is itself a racist act; university controversies cite failure to warn students about blackface content and inadequate apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical media that contains blackface in teaching, require advance warnings, contextual framing, and explicit pedagogical focus on racism to avoid reproducing harm. Be aware of counterarguments invoking academic freedom, but document and weigh harms, student reactions, and institutional commitments to anti-racist practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical use of blackface by Black performers (contextual complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 1840, black performers also were performing in blackface. Blackface minstrelsy gave African-American performers entry into mainstream entertainment; despite reinforcing racist stereotypes, it could be a practical livelihood and a forum for satire, double entendre, and rendering Black music and culture to wider audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical blackface performances in context: examine economic constraints, audience reception (Black and white audiences responded differently), and whether performers used the form to satirize white society or to gain professional opportunities. Avoid simplistic moralizing; consider both harm (stereotype reinforcement) and the complex agency and reception of Black performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity versus caricature in blackface performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which blackface performance drew on authentic black culture and traditions is controversial. Some earlier scholars accepted claims of authenticity; later scholarship (a "third wave") argues blackface drew on black culture but transformed, stereotyped, and caricatured it, producing often racist representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of authenticity critically: require evidence for direct cultural borrowing, track transformation and stereotyping, and foreground scholarship that situates minstrelsy's mixtures of influences. Use this criterion when judging historical claims that minstrel material was 'authentic' black culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darky iconography and commercial/consumer depictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Darky iconography (googly-eyed, inky skin, exaggerated lips, bright teeth) became common in entertainment, children's literature, toys, cartoons, advertising, and product branding; NAACP campaigned to end such portrayals and they largely disappeared in the U.S. by the 1950s onward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating imagery in branding or consumer goods, identify classic darky motifs and consider whether their continued use constitutes racist caricature. Historical evidence of harm, public campaigns (e.g., NAACP), and eventual removal/renaming of products (e.g., 'Darkie' → 'Darlie') are relevant indicators for remedial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating cultural-tradition characters resembling blackface (e.g., Zwarte Piet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like Zwarte Piet (Black Petes) in Dutch/Belgian Sinterklaas traditions wear makeup and attire similar to American blackface; debates focus on origins (Moorish page boy vs chimney soot story), resemblance to archetypal US blackface, and the servant/white figure dynamics. Responses range from gradual toning down (soot smears) to phased removal on public broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess such traditions by examining historical origins, visual and interpersonal dynamics (servant vs master), local public opinion, and reform efforts (e.g., switching to soot smears). Metrics of acceptability include polls, broadcaster policies, and government or civic statements; consider international and cultural-sensitivity perspectives while documenting harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: International variation in tolerance and criticism of blackface
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackface has different histories and levels of tolerance worldwide (examples from the Arab world, Australia, Belgium/Netherlands, Canada, China). In some regions it was common and uncriticized historically; in others recent uses have provoked severe criticism and apologies, linked to reinforcing stereotypes and legacy of slavery or racial hierarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating instances of blackface globally, account for local histories (e.g., trans-Saharan slave trade, colonial legacies), timing (e.g., Ramadan programming), and reactions (public outcry, apologies). Do not assume ideological uniformity; document local debates, institutional responses, and cross-cultural trade/tourism effects that shape sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and institutional responses to blackface incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to blackface controversies include expulsions, apologies, content removal (e.g., streaming platforms pulling episodes), resignations, public debate over academic freedom, and shifts in public broadcasting policy. High-profile examples: expelled students for racially insensitive TikTok, Netflix removing an episode featuring blackface, Justin Trudeau admitting to wearing brownface/brownface photos causing political fallout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative dimension to anticipate and judge appropriate institutional actions: disciplinary measures, content advisories, removals, public apologies, policy changes, and debates balancing free expression with anti-racist commitments. Consider precedent cases and proportionality of responses.
